title: Meeting Lester Young with Basie in Los Angeles; Herschel Evans and Dick Wilson
summary: He first met Lester in 1937 with Basie and describes tenor players Herschel Evans and Dick Wilson.

blocks.x: So the first time you met Lester was
And where was it that you met him?

Here in Los Angeles, when they came out here. And this was a say around '37. When they made "Swinging the Blues" and "Taxi War Dance", "Every Tub", "Sent for you Yesterday and Here you come Today"; everything they did was good. "Rock-a-bye Basie", you know. And then later on, "The World is Mad", "Harvard Blues", did you ever hear Don Byas play the Harvard Blues with Basie? (Whistle). He told a beautiful story on that. But the band, the reed section was like Lester Young and Herschel Evans. Now Herschel Evans took on the appearance of a school teacher, you know professor, a Doctor or something, you know. He was always erect. Rimless glasses. Immaculate. And he had a beautiful sound, you know, I mean like related somewhat to Coleman's sound, Coleman Hawkins. Only it was a might bit smaller. But had he lived, I imagine his sound would have gotten much larger. And he was the one that played "Blue and Sentimental" and Lester Young played clarinet on that side. Speaking of tenor-players, there a, was another tenor player, Dick Wilson, out of Andy Kirk's Band. But he -- you could barely hear him. He had to be miked, you know; but the things that came out of his horn sounded like snakes. It was a very, he was a very, very nice looking young man, he was an ex-football player from college. He was with Andy Kirk and he was from

Seattle, Washington. And his mother died and that was his only living relative and when she died and left everything to him. He went bananas. He just went out to lunch. It was a long time before he rejoined Kirk. Then when he did join Kirk, he turned Alcoholic(?) alcoholic, drug addict, you name it, whatever you had to offer, he wanted some of it.
He would come off the band stand with one pants leg rolled up like he had been riding a bicycle. That's where he was scratching. (Laughter.) But he could play that tenor.
